title: Eigenvalue and Eigenvector: Av = lambda v
quickIdea: An eigenvector is a nonzero vector that the matrix only stretches, shrinks or flips, never turns; the factor it is multiplied by is its eigenvalue.
remember: The definition is Av = lambda v with v not equal to 0. The zero vector is excluded because A0 = 0 = lambda 0 holds for every lambda, which would make every number an eigenvalue.
The eigenvalue may be 0. A singular matrix has 0 as an eigenvalue, and its eigenvectors for 0 are the nonzero vectors of the null space of A.
The eigenvector is not unique: if v is an eigenvector for lambda then so is every nonzero multiple c v. Only the line through v is determined, not the vector.
Av parallel to v includes the antiparallel case, so lambda may be negative; lambda = 0 collapses the vector onto the origin.
A real matrix may have complex eigenvalues, and the eigenvectors for them are then complex vectors.

example.work: Ax = (2+1, 1+2) = (3,3) = 3 (1,1), so x keeps its line and is scaled by 3. Ay = (2,1), which is not a multiple of (1,0), so y does not keep its line.
example.answer: x is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 3; y is not an eigenvector. The other eigenvalue of A is 1, with eigenvector (1,-1).

gateAngle: GATE rarely asks for the definition. It hands you a matrix and a vector and asks whether the vector is an eigenvector, as in 2015 Set 3 Q.15, or it states an eigenpair and asks what follows. Substituting into Av = lambda v is faster and safer than expanding a characteristic equation, and it also tells you which eigenvalue the vector belongs to.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: A = [[1,1],[1,-1]] and v = (1,0). Is v an eigenvector of A?
variations.answer: No. Av = (1,1), and (1,1) is not a multiple of (1,0).
variations.why: The definition is checked by one matrix-vector product, not by solving the characteristic equation; the eigenvectors of this A are (1,1+sqrt2) and (1,1-sqrt2) up to scale, and neither lies on the x axis.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Why does the definition insist that the eigenvector is nonzero, when the equation Av = lambda v would still be true for v = 0?
variations.answer: Because A0 = 0 = lambda 0 for every lambda and every A, so allowing v = 0 would make every scalar an eigenvalue of every matrix and the concept would carry no information.
variations.why: The definition has to pin down a property of A, and only nonzero v can do that.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: A is 3x3 and A v = -2v for v = (1,0,1). What is the eigenvalue, and is (3,0,3) also an eigenvector?
variations.answer: The eigenvalue is -2, and (3,0,3) = 3v is also an eigenvector for -2.
variations.why: The sign of the eigenvalue is read off the equation directly, and eigenvectors come in whole lines: every nonzero multiple works.

trap.what: Reading 'parallel' as 'pointing the same way', so a negative eigenvalue is missed, and counting v = 0 as an eigenvector because the equation holds.
trap.why: Av = lambda v permits lambda < 0, which reverses the vector while keeping its line, and it excludes v = 0 by definition.
trap.counterexample: A = [[0,1],[1,0]] sends (1,-1) to (-1,1) = -1 times (1,-1), so -1 is an eigenvalue even though the vector turns round. And A0 = 0 for this A and for every other matrix, so 0 cannot be counted.

check.question: A = [[3,0],[0,3]]. How many distinct eigenvalues does A have, and which vectors are its eigenvectors?
check.answer: One distinct eigenvalue, 3, and every nonzero vector in the plane is an eigenvector for it.
check.explanation: A = 3I multiplies every vector by 3, so every line is kept. This is the extreme case behind GATE CSE 2026 Set 1 Q.3, where the maximum multiplicity of an eigenvalue of an n x n matrix is n.
